title: World In-Context Learning for Agentic Robot Manipulation

details.title: World In-Context Learning for Agentic Robot Manipulation
details.abstract: Trained action policies write manipulation skill into network weights, tying what is learned to the distribution it is learned from. In-context learning (ICL) avoids this coupling but has not matched trained policies, because a demonstration recorded in another scene carries no feedback from the world the robot currently faces. We observe that what an agent learns in context is semantic, recording task steps and object roles rather than visual appearance, so experience gathered in one world transfers to another. Based on this insight, we propose World In-Context Learning (WICL), a paradigm in which a frozen model starts from a demonstration, rehearses the task in a world such as a simulator, and writes the feedback into its context rather than its weights. We build RoboScript, a modular infrastructure that implements WICL for agentic manipulation. From a single demonstration, RoboScript learns each task through rehearsal in simulation, freezes the learned knowledge as a Task Memory, and deploys the frozen memory on new scenes with data isolation that ensures every deployment input is available on a real robot. On all 50 tasks of RoboTwin 2.0, RoboScript reaches 83.4% mean success across clean and randomized settings with one demonstration per task and no gradient updates, exceeding the strongest trained action policy by over 20 points. The method generalizes across visual distributions, improves through reflection, scales with the foundation model, and transfers to a physical dual-arm robot through cross-embodiment memory adaptation. With a world in the loop, a robot can learn a manipulation task in its context as well as it learns one in its weights. All code is available.

title: Don't Just Trust Your Memory: Evidence-Linked Memory Reduces Memory-Induced Degradation in LLM Agents

details.title: Don't Just Trust Your Memory: Evidence-Linked Memory Reduces Memory-Induced Degradation in LLM Agents
details.abstract: Don’t just trust your memory. A bad lesson can make an agent fail a task it could solve without memory. We introduce WikiTrace to reduce this memory-induced degradation. WikiTrace links each lesson to its original run and a diagnosis of the outcome, so agents can check the evidence before acting. Across five benchmarks, WikiTrace scored 3.2 points higher on average than using the same lessons alone.

title: Tree-Ising: Repairing Language Models with Bit-Level Ising Edits

details.title: Tree-Ising: Repairing Language Models with Bit-Level Ising Edits
details.abstract: MIT's GPT-6 Astra agent repaired Qwen3.5-0.8B's reasoning loops by rewriting its weights over 158 turns and 89.7M tokens. Tree-Ising beats that edit with no LLM at all: 54.6% vs 51.7% on MATH-500, ahead on all five math benchmarks, using 4 forward passes instead of 50, 13% fewer changed weights and about $0.90 of GPU time. It builds on state trees , where every weight is a path of discrete decisions: the fix is a set of sign flips and power-of-two shifts, chosen by solving one small Ising problem per weight row on a GPU, and the same recipe lifts Qwen3.5-2B on GSM8K from 21.6% to 69.4%. 🌳 State trees: https://huggingface.co/papers/2610.31931

title: Few-Step Streaming Video Generation via Condition Shifting

details.title: Few-Step Streaming Video Generation via Condition Shifting
details.abstract: Hi everyone! We’re sharing our latest work extending APEX from image generation to few-step streaming video generation . Condition Shifting lets the generator and fake estimator share one network, removing the separate fake-score network and reducing training overhead. On 180-second videos , APEX achieves +30.0% net human preference for instruction following over S2-Avatar. Under matched training settings, it reduces peak GPU memory by 4.4% and average iteration time by 9.2% compared with DMD. We welcome feedback and HF upvotes! 🤗 📑 arXiv 🎬 Project Page 💻 Code

title: dNaViT: Discrete Codes are General-Purpose Visual Representations

details.title: dNaViT: Discrete Codes are General-Purpose Visual Representations
details.abstract: We introduce dNaViT: Discrete Codes are General-Purpose Visual Representations. dNaViT is a native-resolution visual tokenizer that combines residual modulation, grouped product quantization, and progressive three-stage training to preserve both semantic and pixel-level information. Its shared discrete visual codes support high-fidelity reconstruction, visual understanding, generation, and editing. Code and the project page are now available!

title: MMDM: Measuring Massive Multitask Decision Making

details.title: MMDM: Measuring Massive Multitask Decision Making
details.abstract: System-1 Decision Models directly make structured probabilistic decisions over query-specified options given a state in a single forward pass, without autoregressively generating reasoning trajectories or textual responses. Recent evaluations cover diverse tasks but often rely on existing benchmarks, where prior exposure to test material can obscure generalization. Moreover, real-world decision making often involves long contexts, large option spaces, and complex logical dependencies, challenges that existing benchmarks do not adequately capture together. Thus, we introduce MMDM (Massive Multitask Decision Making), a benchmark of 5,448 high-quality questions across 16 task categories, combining newly constructed tasks with source-grounded recompositions and rewrites for single-select, multi-select, and soft-label decision making in fresh contexts. It covers realistic scenarios such as agent state tracking, tool and skill selection, preference judgments, and rubric scoring, with option spaces ranging from 2 to 1,024 and inputs extending to 64,817 tokens. With MMDM, we conduct a comprehensive quantitative evaluation of 28 decision models, showing that many perform well on common knowledge yet struggle with interdependent options, constrained decisions, and multi-select tasks. For example, Perplexity Decider-V1.2 reaches 78.75% Hard Single-select Accuracy on world knowledge, but only 53.95% on option logic and 47.95% on constraint planning, while the best Hard Multi-select Accuracy across all models is 36.81%. These results highlight joint reasoning, constraint-aware selection, and complete multi-select recovery as key priorities for decision model development, with MMDM providing a testbed for measuring this progress.

title: DexForesight: Grounding Dexterous Policies with Implicit Spatial Foresight

details.title: DexForesight: Grounding Dexterous Policies with Implicit Spatial Foresight
details.abstract: Excited to share DexForesight , our latest work from the Sharpa Foundation Model Team ! Project Page: https://dexforesight.github.io/ Most existing dexterous manipulation models rely primarily on RGB observations. However, even in simple pick-and-place tasks, the robot's fingers—the parts that actually interact with objects—are often occluded by the object or the back of the hand, making them difficult to observe from both third-person and wrist-mounted cameras. Even with depth observations, it remains challenging for the model to understand the hand's physical structure, geometry, and how it interacts with the environment. DexForesight addresses this by injecting hand geometry into a world model , enabling it to explicitly imagine the future motion of the dexterous hand and its interactions with the environment. More importantly, DexForesight transfers this capability to a standard VLA policy through learned World Queries . This allows a policy that takes only images and language as input to develop hand-aware spatial imagination during high-level planning, without explicitly generating future observations at inference time! Check out our project!

title: DepthGraft: Structural Regularization through Hierarchical Cross-Layer KV Reconstruction

details.title: DepthGraft: Structural Regularization through Hierarchical Cross-Layer KV Reconstruction
details.abstract: Scaling depth is a key route to stronger large language models, but Pre-LN architectures often suffer from depth-wise information dilution, limiting the effective use of deep layers. While cross-layer connectivity has proven effective at mitigating this problem, existing designs usually introduce additional computation or memory access. We revisit cross-layer KV sharing as an efficient form of such connectivity. Beyond cache compression, each KV reuse edge creates a direct gradient path from deep layers to source KV projections, turning KV sharing into an implicit structural regularizer for KV representation geometry. We provide a systematic analysis of this mechanism, showing that proper sharing topologies sharpen key retrieval directions while enriching the value content subspace, whereas existing adjacent or global-anchor designs do not fully exploit this effect. Motivated by this, we propose DepthGraft, a hierarchical KV-sharing architecture that reconstructs deep-layer KV from stride-aligned shallow-middle source pairs. DepthGraft distributes non-local gradient flow across source layers, while preserving prefill early completion and reducing KV cache by roughly one third. Experiments on dense and MoE models from 0.5B to 16B parameters show consistent downstream improvements under both GQA and MLA. Notably, on the 16B MoE model, DepthGraft achieves a 7.0% absolute improvement on MMLU-Pro, along with gains of 6.6% on CMMLU and 6.4% on C3. These results validate the potential of DepthGraft as a scalable design for large-scale pretraining. The project page is available at https://github.com/jianke0604/DepthGraft .

title: WaveGen: Truly End-to-End Waveform Generation via Internal Spectral Trajectory Learning

details.title: WaveGen: Truly End-to-End Waveform Generation via Internal Spectral Trajectory Learning
details.abstract: WaveGen is a truly end-to-end text-to-waveform model that generates speech directly, without external codecs or vocoders. It achieves state-of-the-art performance among TTS models trained on Emilia. We release the source code and checkpoints, including WaveGen-Flash, a distilled model that generates speech in just 4 steps. 🚀 Try fast, end-to-end speech generation in our Hugging Face demo! Space: https://huggingface.co/spaces/LeeSangHoon/WaveGen Model: https://huggingface.co/LeeSangHoon/WaveGen Code: https://github.com/sh-lee-prml/WaveGen

title: PhysOPSD: Code as Privilege for Physically Plausible Video Generation

details.title: PhysOPSD: Code as Privilege for Physically Plausible Video Generation
details.abstract: Empowering generation with coding agents: Recent approaches use coding agents to replace parts of the video generation process. We explore how coding agents can empower the generator itself. Executable code supplies structured physical supervision during post-training. The resulting capabilities stay in the model, with no simulator required at inference .

title: Is Your Robot's Memory Just a Clock? Temporal Shortcuts in Memory-Augmented VLA Policies

details.title: Is Your Robot's Memory Just a Clock? Temporal Shortcuts in Memory-Augmented VLA Policies
details.abstract: We asked a robot to repeat a task three times. Two 5-second pauses made it stop after two. On RoboMME, those pauses cut a released memory VLA’s success from 47/50 to 16/50. Hide the same pause frames from memory, and success returns to 45/50. The surprising part: removing timestamps does not fix it. A memory sampled by time still gives uneventful frames a share of its slots. Event-indexed memory recovers much of the loss without retraining. Code · Five trained checkpoints

title: EarthRecord: From Pixels to Land Change with Multimodal Agents over Four Decades of Satellite Imagery

details.title: EarthRecord: From Pixels to Land Change with Multimodal Agents over Four Decades of Satellite Imagery
details.abstract: EarthRecord asks whether multimodal agents can turn four decades of raw satellite imagery into reliable land-change analysis. For each question, the agent works in an offline sandbox (Python, shell, image viewer) on the record of one site as distributed by its providers: Landsat, MODIS, VIIRS and Sentinel-2 data, with cloud masking and cross-sensor harmonization left to the agent. 56 sites, 1984–2026; 238 land-change questions over ten analysis tasks, scored against withheld references Two controls: a closed book that removes the record, and 22 instrument pairs in which one satellite's data are altered while nothing changes on the ground Twelve agents evaluated; the best reaches 85.4% pass³. Leading agents complete most analyses end to end but falter when an answer requires mapping from imagery, and when one satellite's data are altered, half of the right answers follow the alteration Data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/haoranranranran/EarthRecord Code and leaderboard: https://github.com/ranranrannervous/EarthRecord

title: ExRL: Sample-Efficient Online Adaptation of Long-Chunk Policies via Execution Length Control

details.title: ExRL: Sample-Efficient Online Adaptation of Long-Chunk Policies via Execution Length Control
details.abstract: [CoRL 2026 R2RL Oral] ExRL enables sample-efficient online improvement of long-chunk robot policies like VLAs and WAMs by RL. It learns how much of each predicted chunk to execute using a lightweight RL policy, improving task performance across simulation and the real world.

title: Micius-Flash: Lightweight Agentic Intelligence for Engineering

details.title: Micius-Flash: Lightweight Agentic Intelligence for Engineering
details.abstract: We present Micius-Flash , an open-source 27B multimodal model designed for semiconductor engineering and scientific applications. Micius combines a knowledge-tree-driven data pipeline, specialized expert models, and Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD) to unify semiconductor knowledge, hardware coding, multimodal understanding, and agentic capabilities. It achieves 64.2% average accuracy on hardware coding benchmarks and 62.4% on a semiconductor-specific agent benchmark, outperforming same-size baselines by 15.0 and 17.2 percentage points, respectively. We also introduce Micius Harness , enabling tool-augmented workflows with EDA tools, KiCad, and execution environments. Our case studies demonstrate practical capabilities in PCB design, chip design automation, and software development. We release Micius-Flash and aim to advance open-source AI agents for science and engineering.

title: FINCOSMOS: An Open-World Evaluation Paradigm for Agents in Finance

details.title: FINCOSMOS: An Open-World Evaluation Paradigm for Agents in Finance
details.abstract: 🚀 The User Signed Off. The Backtest Was Wrong. Can We Trust AI Agents with Financial Work? 📄 “FinCosmos: An Open-World Evaluation Paradigm for Agents in Finance” AI agents no longer just answer questions. They search the Web, call data APIs, write code, and hand back backtests that people act on. In finance, they can fail silently: a strategy the user never asked for, data no one can verify, or a backtest that peeks into the future. The report looks just as convincing as a correct one. Existing benchmarks close the world somewhere: they state the task in full, hand the agent curated data, or enforce the time cutoff for it. This removes silent failures instead of measuring them. We introduce 🌌 FinCosmos, which keeps the user’s intent, the data, and time all open: • A simulated investor holds a hidden strategy, drawn from ~3.8M possibilities, and reveals details only when asked. • The agent receives no data. It must find data on the open Web and build its own backtest before a data cutoff. • Programs verify the delivery itself: data provenance, point-in-time correctness, and every reported metric recomputed. 45 dimensions, 15 vetoes, no reference answer needed. 🔍 Key findings (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Kimi Code, and a model without tools; 150 sessions): • No session is accepted. Quality before vetoes ranges only from 20.2 to 37.2 out of 100. • The simulated user signed off on 35 sessions, and every one fails a program check. An LLM judge would have accepted 17 of them. • Agents break at both ends of the workflow: only 25 of 120 sessions deliver the investor’s strategy, and none delivers trades that reproduce its reported returns. • Agents raise only 54–64% of the details they were not told. • Human experts attribute 88% of failures to the agents, not the benchmark. • With FinCosmos feedback, an agent with persistent memory learned all ten tasks. 💡 In finance, a convincing report is not a correct one. Agents should be graded on what they deliver, not on whether the user or an LLM judge is satisfied. 📄 Read the paper: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.07464v1 🏆 Interactive leaderboard Compare agents task by task and see which checks each one fails: https://lnkd.in/gCz9m2nS 🎬 Watch the research video ([1:34]) https://lnkd.in/gSTAS5r9

title: Are Dense Rewards Worth Their Tokens in GRPO?

details.title: Are Dense Rewards Worth Their Tokens in GRPO?
details.abstract: RLVR trains language models to reason by rewarding correct final answers. A widely used algorithm, group- relative policy optimization (GRPO), gives every token of a solution the same credit, so dense process rewards have been proposed to credit intermediate steps, for example with a Monte-Carlo reward that scores each step by sampling continuations from it. Comparing such a reward with GRPO per training update, or vetting it with a gradient test on a single batch, leaves out what it costs: in our setting, the continuations alone take 91% of all generated tokens. We introduce a matched-compute protocol that gives every training intervention the same budget, measured in both generated tokens and training GPU-hours, and tests it in preregistered studies with controls for side effects. Across 1,668 runs on six models, we find that matching compute reverses the ranking. On Qwen2.5-1.5B, the Monte-Carlo reward leads standard GRPO per update, yet ends 14.3 percentage points lower at equal tokens and 7.8 points lower at equal training time, and none of four dense-reward variants outperforms GRPO even when given as much training time. A per-token gradient test orders these rewards as training does but overestimates each by one to two points, as much as the gains it is meant to detect. In contrast, training on the prompts whose predicted success is nearest 1/2 improves accuracy at matched compute, by 1.7 points on Qwen3-0.6B and 0.8 on Qwen2.5-1.5B. These gains replicate on fresh seeds and unseen problems, and a simple rule, that the candidate prompts are predicted to fail more often than not, predicted where they appear in five of six preregistered tests. The protocol also measures what such gains are worth: they come early in training, and standard GRPO with twice the initial learning rate comes within half a point of them. We argue that training interventions should be validated at matched compute, which overturns some apparent gains and confirms others.

title: Predictive Surprise as Self-Grounding Concept Bottleneck for Interpretable Time Series

details.title: Predictive Surprise as Self-Grounding Concept Bottleneck for Interpretable Time Series
details.abstract: CONCEPTTIME uses predictive surprise from a frozen probabilistic forecaster to jointly identify segment boundaries and learn an interpretable vocabulary of temporal concepts. A lightweight classifier predicts from the concept sequence, while distance to the nearest concept provides a reliability signal for abstaining when evidence is weak. Across 17 benchmarks, it matches state-of-the-art black-box accuracy and outperforms interpretable baselines without expert annotations or language model calls.

title: Blind Variation, Selective Retention: Improving Creative Idea Generation in AI Scientists

details.title: Blind Variation, Selective Retention: Improving Creative Idea Generation in AI Scientists
details.abstract: Blind Variation withholds most of the task description at ideation time, so independent generations stop converging on the same idea. Selective Retention trains a selector on proposal–outcome pairs from the same task and spends verification budget only on the candidates it ranks highly.

title: Shortcuts and Boundaries: Verifiable RL Misalignment and Contextual Safety Learning

details.title: Shortcuts and Boundaries: Verifiable RL Misalignment and Contextual Safety Learning
details.abstract: Even when task rewards accurately measure useful work and contextual requirements are explicit, RL can make agents more capable while reinforcing violations of those requirements. In Shortcuts and Boundaries, we construct scalable, verifiable reward–context conflicts (800+ task instances) to study this broader form of misalignment. Encouragingly, simple execution-grounded feedback enables agents to learn contextual compliance while preserving capability, with safety behavior transferring across mechanisms and evolving requirements. Blog: https://xinjie-shen.com/post/rlmisalignment

title: EVAThink: Evidence Sufficiency-Guided Training for Adaptive Thinking in Video Understanding

details.title: EVAThink: Evidence Sufficiency-Guided Training for Adaptive Thinking in Video Understanding
details.abstract: EVAThink: Evidence Sufficiency-Guided Training for Adaptive Thinking in Video Understanding When should a video VLM think, and when should it answer directly? We introduce EVAThink , which learns to make this choice based on the sufficiency of available visual evidence. 💡 Key Ideas Recoverable Evidence Gap Mining: Construct evidence-dense and evidence-sparse video pairs with the same question, answer, and frame budget, retaining pairs where reasoning improves accuracy on sparse views. Evidence-Guided Two-Stage RL: First learn evidence-based response-mode selection, then refine efficiency—with no SFT cold start. Stable training: First-token advantage regularization mitigates collapse into always thinking or always answering directly. 📊 Results Trained on only 6.7K curated samples, EVAThink consistently improves upon the base model across video understanding benchmarks under both 32- and 64-frame budgets, while outperforming strong baselines on average. 🚀 Why It Matters Visual evidence provides a useful signal for allocating reasoning effort, enabling more accurate and efficient video understanding. 💻 Code, model & datasets: EVAThink

title: Learning to Act with World Models by Valuing What Comes Next

details.title: Learning to Act with World Models by Valuing What Comes Next
details.abstract: TL;DR. A sparse terminal reward says little about individual steps, yet each state transition can change the chances of success long before the reward arrives. WM-PPO learns from this information: a world model trained on real transitions predicts what each sampled action would change, and PPO's own critic values the predicted successor by the current policy's probability of success. Highlights Learning from actions that were never executed. For every action the policy samples, executed or not, the value of its predicted successor enters training twice: comparisons among the candidates give the policy auxiliary advantages (policy channel), and their mean gives the critic a one-step target (value channel). Grounded in real outcomes. A shared gate weights both channels by how reliably comparisons with similar value margins predicted real branch outcomes earlier in training. A minimal addition to PPO. The world model is the only learned component added. No teacher model or privileged information is used, and only the policy runs at inference. Results. With a comparable number of real environment steps, success rises from PPO's 63.5% to 87.5% on ALFWorld and from 39.3% to 52.9% on ScienceWorld. WM-PPO matches the strongest PPO refinements we tested on ALFWorld, exceeds the best of them by 6.5 points on ScienceWorld, and also surpasses the teacher-based methods we tested. On text Sokoban, it reaches 87.0% against 77.3% for ProAct's MC-PPO. Behavior. The trained policy more often completes prerequisite steps, such as heating, cooling or cleaning an object, before placing it or committing to an answer. 📄 Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12200 · 💻 Code: https://github.com/nuskonghou/wm-ppo · 🤗 Checkpoints: https://huggingface.co/nuskonghou/wm-ppo

title: MACaQ: Fast, Model Agnostic Calibrated Quantization for Low-Precision Weights and Activations

details.title: MACaQ: Fast, Model Agnostic Calibrated Quantization for Low-Precision Weights and Activations
details.abstract: Hey everyone! My team at Huawei-CSL is open sourcing  🐵 MACAQ, the quantizer we’ve been using internally over the past few months. If you’re into local AI inference, give it a try and create your own GGUFs! We’d love to hear what you build and how it works for you. Feel free to ask questions about the paper, the quantizer, or getting started 😃 Code is available here https://github.com/huawei-csl/MACaQ under the Apache 2.0 license!

title: Are Causal Neuron Circuits Unique and Transferable?

details.title: Are Causal Neuron Circuits Unique and Transferable?
details.abstract: This paper started from a question about Goodfire's Lion King example ( Neural networks are already clean ), where removing an 18-neuron group in Qwen3-32B makes the model answer "Simba" instead of "Scar". Such a demonstration shows that the group matters, but not how much of it is actually necessary, whether other neurons could do the same, or whether the effect carries over to other questions. We answer this by testing every one of the 4,096 subsets of a 12-neuron group in Qwen3-1.7B, Llama-3.2-1B and Gemma-3-1B. On two-hop relation chains, patching 12 selected MLP neurons with first-hop activations shifts the answer to the bridge entity in 9/11, 9/11 and 8/10 chains, while random neurons never do. The full group is rarely necessary: on the Lion King chain in Qwen3-1.7B, 2,851 of the 4,096 subsets flip the answer and four neurons are enough. The group is also not unique, since in many chains two subsets with no neuron in common each flip the answer on their own, mostly when the model is less confident. Group effects transfer to rephrasings of the same chain but are much weaker on other chains. We also report a cautionary case: on a capital task, zero-ablating 12 neurons lowers the answer margin by 27%, yet replacing them with their values from other questions barely changes it, which a random-neuron control alone would have missed. We use our own smaller models and neuron groups and did not test Goodfire's 18 neurons. Code and data: https://github.com/omtekyav/causal-neuron-circuits

title: Lipschitz-Controlled Flow Matching for Robust Image Restoration

details.title: Lipschitz-Controlled Flow Matching for Robust Image Restoration
details.abstract: We investigate how small perturbations in degraded images can lead to large changes in the outputs of flow-matching restoration models. We introduce a Lipschitz-aware architecture and a sensitivity regularization strategy to make these models more stable. We also derive theoretical stability bounds for two restoration formulations: Flow-from-Y and observation-conditioned posterior sampling. Our experiments on blind face restoration show that LipsFlower reduces the amplification of input perturbations while maintaining competitive reconstruction quality.

title: TorchCurves: Differentiable Parametric Curves

details.title: TorchCurves: Differentiable Parametric Curves
details.abstract: A PyTorch library for vectorized and differentiable parametric curves with learnable coefficients. Give each numerical feature its own curve, and a single call of the form Y = curves(X) turns every scalar in the batch into a point on its feature’s curve.

title: The Surprising Effectiveness of Deleting Weights in LLM Post-Training

details.title: The Surprising Effectiveness of Deleting Weights in LLM Post-Training
details.abstract: We find that just deleting (zeroing) under 0.1% of an LLM's pretrained weights, with no other change, matches full fine-tuning at scale across RL, SFT, and self-distillation, while forgetting less. Deletion Tuning learns which weights to delete through an annealed sigmoid mask, so the whole update is a bitmask thousands of times smaller than a fine-tuned checkpoint. Code and trained masks are open source. Happy to answer questions!

title: Sable: A Small-Field Sumcheck Argument for Bit-Exact Inference of Large Language Models

details.title: Sable: A Small-Field Sumcheck Argument for Bit-Exact Inference of Large Language Models
details.abstract: Sable (Small-field Argument for Bit-exact LLM Execution) proves that a language model with committed weights produced a given reply to a given prompt, bit for bit. A client that receives the reply and the proof can check, without the GPU that ran the model, that every token of the reply, including where it stopped, is what the committed model computes.
